issues.explanation: 'Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen' is a plausible PTSD threat cue in some cases, but here it is weakly connected to the selected triggers and memory content. The trigger set emphasizes locations and nightmare residue from a mugging, while the memory items concern fragmented recall and guilt. Silence as the key danger signal is insufficiently anchored in the rest of this robbery-based profile and stands out as an unintegrated threat item.

It is not impossible, but in this item set it appears insufficiently connected to the trauma-specific trigger pattern.

issues.explanation: 'Lost connection to my community and culture' is hard to reconcile as a primary negative appraisal for a 29-year-old married male after a mugging/robbery when the other appraisals are mistrust and isolation. Mistrust and isolation fit robbery-related PTSD, but community/cultural disconnection suggests a different psychosocial theme not supported by the triggers, memory, or threat items in this profile.

vignette:
Rohan, a 29-year-old South Asian man, had always prided himself on his steady hands and keen eye as a painter, but now, six months after the mugging, his world felt perpetually out of focus. The incident had occurred late one evening as he walked home from a client’s house, his heavy bag of tools slung over his shoulder, down a dimly lit alley he’d taken as a shortcut. He remembered the sudden grab from behind, the hand clamped over his mouth, the glint of a knife at his throat, and the guttural snarl of one of his two attackers before he was shoved against a brick wall, his head connecting with a sickening thud. They vanished with his bag and his week’s earnings, leaving him disoriented and alone.

In the immediate aftermath, Rohan struggled to process the event. He felt like he was only remembering parts of what happened, disjointed flashes of movement and sound, while the rest was frustratingly missing, as if his mind had deliberately obscured the worst details. This incomplete picture of the event left him with an intense guilt on recall, convinced that if he could just remember every detail, he could somehow understand what he did wrong or how he could have prevented it. The harder he tried to deliberately remember what happened, the more elusive and fragmented the full memory became.

Soon, his daily life began to be punctuated by potent triggers. Waking up from a nightmare, his heart pounding and drenched in sweat, Rohan would find the lingering dread of the dream residue immediately plunging him into a state where his body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger. He began to constantly scan his surroundings for signs of danger, particularly when his work as a painter took him to new physical locations, like construction sites or client homes in unfamiliar parts of the city, which became powerful spatial triggers. These external cues, whether the unexpected clang of metal or the dim lighting of a new street, would often wrench him back to the moment of the attack, bringing with them a sudden, vivid flash of the knife or the attacker's face. An intrusive memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, a flash of the knife or the attacker's face, would not only send his body on alert and make him feel a surge of irritability, but also make it even harder to access the full, coherent memory he desperately sought, intensifying his sense of an incomplete picture.

This constant state of vigilance and the relentless intrusion of these triggers, constantly reminding him of his vulnerability, solidified Rohan's growing belief that people can't be trusted. He had always been an open person, but now he was certain that he couldn't rely on other people, viewing any potential dependence as a dangerous vulnerability. This appraisal, that he couldn't rely on others, began to fuel his pervasive body on alert, making him even more prone to scanning for danger in every interaction, even with strangers on the street. This deep-seated mistrust then began to make him perceive even innocuous situations as potential threats, transforming routine occurrences into triggers that sent his body into overdrive. He found himself thinking, "Why would I put myself out there when I know people are inherently unreliable?" This led him to feel increasingly isolated and set apart from others, even from his wife, as he retreated further into himself, convinced that no one could truly understand or help him.

The incomplete picture of what happened, combined with the intense guilt on recall, kept his nervous system in a perpetual state of agitation, making his body feel constantly on alert. This internal struggle, particularly the guilt, only reinforced his mistrust in himself and others. The constant scanning for danger, a direct consequence of his heightened threat response, made him hyper-vigilant to spatial triggers, meaning any dimly lit street or unexpected shadow could immediately escalate his internal alarm system. Furthermore, his reluctance to discuss the event, stemming from his fragmented memory and guilt, would often lead to him avoiding conversations or places, which in turn could become new triggers for his distress.

Rohan’s irritability began to manifest as angry outbursts at his wife, who struggled to understand his sudden shifts in mood and his increasing withdrawal. His work as a painter, which once brought him joy, became a source of immense anxiety. Visiting new client homes or working late hours in public spaces, which were now potent spatial triggers, meant his body was constantly on alert. He found himself rushing through jobs, unable to focus, and often leaving early, which affected his income and reputation. The accumulating strain on his marriage, coupled with the financial stress from his inability to work consistently, finally brought Rohan to seek help. He arrived feeling exhausted, perpetually on edge, and deeply alone, still grappling with the conviction that people couldn't be trusted, yet desperate for some relief from the relentless tension that had become his daily companion. His greatest fear was that this constant state of vigilance and mistrust would eventually erode everything he held dear, leaving him truly isolated, with no one left to even pretend to rely on.
